findings.claim: Duplicate discriminator values abort compilation and are only surfaced later (and as a different error type) by the interpreter, so the new comment's "whose own map build reports it" guarantee is timing- and type-dependent.
findings.rationale: The new comment asserts that declining to compile hands the collision back to the interpreter, "whose own map build reports it." That only holds if the interpreter builds its discriminator map on every path the compiled path would have covered; in core the disc map is built lazily on first parse and the failure surfaces as a plain Error, not a ZodCompileUnsupportedError. Net effect for a caller: a schema with genuinely colliding discriminator values gets no compile-time diagnostic, silently loses the fast path, and only fails at first parse with an unrelated error type. Worth confirming the interpreter throws unconditionally; if it instead tolerates duplicates with first-match semantics, this compile-time rejection changes observable behavior rather than preserving it. Low-to-moderate confidence: depends on interpreter code not visible in this hunk.

findings.claim: The `claimed` de-duplication relies on Set SameValueZero semantics, which can both invent and miss collisions for exotic discriminator values.
findings.rationale: `claimed.has(value)` / `claimed.add(value)` compare with SameValueZero, so `0` and `-0` are treated as the same discriminator (spurious duplicate rejection, losing the fast path), while structurally equal object/array values from different options compare by reference and would be treated as distinct (missed collision, letting the branch chain compile first-match dispatch — exactly the case the new comment claims is guarded against). Also `String(value)` renders `undefined`/symbol discriminators unhelpfully in the error. Low confidence these shapes actually occur in `propValues`, but the comment's claim is only as strong as the equality used here.
